newsitem.title: UK: Invesco likes Latam and East Europe, light in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Invesco likes Latam and East Europe, light in Asia.

text.p: Invesco Asset Management is bullish on Latin America and Eastern Europe but will tread lightly in Southeast Asia amid regional currency uncertainty.

"Our strategy has been to overweight Latin America and Eastern Europe. We have increased our aggressive stance as the months progressed," Francesco Bertoni, head of the fund manager's emerging markets desk, told Reuters.
"The big question is: when do you change that? We think it is early to make a massive move back into Asia."
Invesco, which manages about $3.5 billion in emerging markets equities, recently finished top of the Micropal league tables in emerging markets fund management.

Bertoni sees the round of currency devaluations in Southeast Asia as positive in the long term, particularly for Indonesia and the Philippines, but fears that the currency market carnage may not be at an end.
"Devaluations are wonderful opportunities, but timing is crucial," he said. "Even if values have come back, you are in a situation where three more months of turmoil could make a big difference."

Indonesia and the Philippines will be better positioned than Thailand because they have less foreign borrowings, he said, but until their currencies find a level, interest rates will have to stay high.
But even after the currency turmoil is over, the risk premium demanded by investors in Southeast Asia will have changed profoundly, according to Bertoni.
Because of their former strong relationship to the dollar, investors had largely discounted currency risk in Southeast Asia.
"It will take years to re-establish that. If you look at last year relative valuations of Far East versus Latin America there was a different risk premium that people attached to those investments"
"They wanted to buy Brazil at 10 times (earnings) but were happy to buy Indonesia at 20 times (earnings) because they knew that the investment in Brazil was much more volatile and risky."
"The assumption was that the economies in Asia were always growing and you have little currency risk - those things no longer hold true," he said.
In Latin America, Invesco is overweight on Brazil, Mexico and Peru.
The current account deficit "is a concern, but the potential for falling rates and continued privitisations makes us comfortable with retaining our position in Brazil."
Mexico's attraction is straightforward, he says, as a recovered export sector is twinned with signs of returning consumer demand.
Invesco's other big favourite is Russia, where it has a sizeable seven percent allocation.
"It is not what Russia is doing but what it could do. There is potentially a huge domestic market and a huge export market."
"It will take ages and go up and down in the process, but huge potential is there."
Any major correction in world equity markets will hit emerging markets especially hard, Bertoni said.
But if Wall Street hits a plateau the result could be a sizeable flow of funds into emerging markets, he said.
"In the past people have gone out the risk-reward curve driven by low returns in developed markets. They try to stretch out the normal risk parameters." -- James Saft, London newsroom +171 542 2734
